36:33.ar: وَءَايَةࣱ لَّهُمُ ٱلۡأَرۡضُ ٱلۡمَيۡتَةُ أَحۡيَيۡنَٰهَا وَأَخۡرَجۡنَا مِنۡهَا حَبࣰّ ا فَمِنۡهُ يَأۡكُلُونَ
36:33.en: A token unto them is the dead earth. We revive it, and We bring forth from it grain so that they eat thereof

36:34.ar: وَجَعَلۡنَا فِيهَا جَنَّٰتࣲ مِّن نَّخِيلࣲ وَأَعۡنَٰبࣲ وَفَجَّرۡنَا فِيهَا مِنَ ٱلۡعُيُونِ
36:34.en: And We have placed therein gardens of the date-palm and grapes, and We have caused springs of water to gush forth therein

36:35.ar: لِيَأۡكُلُواْ مِن ثَمَرِهِۦ وَمَا عَمِلَتۡهُ أَيۡدِيهِمۡۚ أَفَلَا يَشۡكُرُونَ
36:35.en: That they may eat of the fruit thereof, and their hands made it not. Will they not, then, give thanks

36:36.ar: سُبۡحَٰنَ ٱلَّذِي خَلَقَ ٱلۡأَزۡوَٰجَ كُلَّهَا مِمَّا تُنۢبِتُ ٱلۡأَرۡضُ وَمِنۡ أَنفُسِهِمۡ وَمِمَّا لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
36:36.en: Glory be to Him Who created all the sexual pairs, of that which the earth groweth, and of themselves, and of that which they know not

36:37.ar: وَءَايَةࣱ لَّهُمُ ٱلَّيۡلُ نَسۡلَخُ مِنۡهُ ٱلنَّهَارَ فَإِذَا هُم مُّظۡلِمُونَ
36:37.en: A token unto them is night. We strip it of the day, and lo! they are in darkness

36:38.ar: وَٱلشَّمۡسُ تَجۡرِي لِمُسۡتَقَرࣲّ لَّهَاۚ ذَٰلِكَ تَقۡدِيرُ ٱلۡعَزِيزِ ٱلۡعَلِيمِ
36:38.en: And the sun runneth on unto a resting-place for him. That is the measuring of the Mighty, the Wise

36:39.ar: وَٱلۡقَمَرَ قَدَّرۡنَٰهُ مَنَازِلَ حَتَّىٰ عَادَ كَٱلۡعُرۡجُونِ ٱلۡقَدِيمِ
36:39.en: And for the moon We have appointed mansions till she return like an old shrivelled palm-leaf

36:40.ar: لَا ٱلشَّمۡسُ يَنۢبَغِي لَهَآ أَن تُدۡرِكَ ٱلۡقَمَرَ وَلَا ٱلَّيۡلُ سَابِقُ ٱلنَّهَارِۚ وَكُلࣱّ فِي فَلَكࣲ يَسۡبَحُونَ
36:40.en: It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor doth the night outstrip the day. They float each in an orbit

36:11.ar: إِنَّمَا تُنذِرُ مَنِ ٱتَّبَعَ ٱلذِّكۡرَ وَخَشِيَ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنَ بِٱلۡغَيۡبِۖ فَبَشِّرۡهُ بِمَغۡفِرَةࣲ وَأَجۡرࣲ كَرِيمٍ
36:11.en: Thou warnest only him who followeth the Reminder and feareth the Beneficent in secret. To him bear tidings of forgiveness and a rich reward

39:30.en: Lo! thou wilt die, and lo! they will die

21:23.ar: لَا يُسۡـَٔلُ عَمَّا يَفۡعَلُ وَهُمۡ يُسۡـَٔلُونَ
21:23.en: He will not be questioned as to that which He doeth, but they will be questioned

42:11.ar: فَاطِرُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۚ جَعَلَ لَكُم مِّنۡ أَنفُسِكُمۡ أَزۡوَٰجࣰ ا وَمِنَ ٱلۡأَنۡعَٰمِ أَزۡوَٰجࣰ ا يَذۡرَؤُكُمۡ فِيهِۚ لَيۡسَ كَمِثۡلِهِۦ شَيۡءࣱۖ وَهُوَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلۡبَصِيرُ
42:11.en: The Creator of the heavens and the earth. He hath made for you pairs of yourselves, and of the cattle also pairs, whereby He multiplieth you. Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer

16:8.ar: وَٱلۡخَيۡلَ وَٱلۡبِغَالَ وَٱلۡحَمِيرَ لِتَرۡكَبُوهَا وَزِينَةࣰۚ وَيَخۡلُقُ مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
16:8.en: And horses and mules and asses (hath He created) that ye may ride them, and for ornament. And He createth that which ye know not

2:129.ar: رَبَّنَا وَٱبۡعَثۡ فِيهِمۡ رَسُولࣰ ا مِّنۡهُمۡ يَتۡلُواْ عَلَيۡهِمۡ ءَايَٰتِكَ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَٱلۡحِكۡمَةَ وَيُزَكِّيهِمۡۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ
2:129.en: Our Lord! And raise up in their midst a messenger from among them who shall recite unto them Thy revelations, and shall instruct them in the Scripture and in wisdom and shall make them grow. Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Mighty, Wise

62:2.ar: هُوَ ٱلَّذِي بَعَثَ فِي ٱلۡأُمِّيِّـۧنَ رَسُولࣰ ا مِّنۡهُمۡ يَتۡلُواْ عَلَيۡهِمۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ وَيُزَكِّيهِمۡ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَٱلۡحِكۡمَةَ وَإِن كَانُواْ مِن قَبۡلُ لَفِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينࣲ‏
62:2.en: He it is Who hath sent among the unlettered ones a messenger of their own, to recite unto them His revelations and to make them grow, and to teach them the Scripture and wisdom, though heretofore they were indeed in error manifest

67:3.ar: ٱلَّذِي خَلَقَ سَبۡعَ سَمَٰوَٰتࣲ طِبَاقࣰ اۖ مَّا تَرَىٰ فِي خَلۡقِ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ مِن تَفَٰوُتࣲۖ فَٱرۡجِعِ ٱلۡبَصَرَ هَلۡ تَرَىٰ مِن فُطُورࣲ‏
67:3.en: Who hath created seven heavens in harmony. Thou (Muhammad) canst see no fault in the Beneficent One's creation; then look again: Canst thou see any rifts

67:4.ar: ثُمَّ ٱرۡجِعِ ٱلۡبَصَرَ كَرَّتَيۡنِ يَنقَلِبۡ إِلَيۡكَ ٱلۡبَصَرُ خَاسِئࣰ ا وَهُوَ حَسِيرࣱ‏
67:4.en: Then look again and yet again, thy sight will return unto thee weakened and made dim

35:24.ar: إِنَّآ أَرۡسَلۡنَٰكَ بِٱلۡحَقِّ بَشِيرࣰ ا وَنَذِيرࣰ اۚ وَإِن مِّنۡ أُمَّةٍ إِلَّا خَلَا فِيهَا نَذِيرࣱ‏
35:24.en: Lo! We have sent thee with the Truth, a bearer of glad tidings and a warner; and there is not a nation but a warner hath passed among them

73:19.ar: إِنَّ هَٰذِهِۦ تَذۡكِرَةࣱۖ فَمَن شَآءَ ٱتَّخَذَ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِۦ سَبِيلًا
73:19.en: Lo! This is a Reminder. Let him who will, then, choose a way unto his Lord

59:24.ar: هُوَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلۡخَٰلِقُ ٱلۡبَارِئُ ٱلۡمُصَوِّرُۖ لَهُ ٱلۡأَسۡمَآءُ ٱلۡحُسۡنَىٰۚ يُسَبِّحُ لَهُۥ مَا فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۖ وَهُوَ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ
59:24.en: He is Allah, the Creator, the Shaper out of naught, the Fashioner. His are the most beautiful names. All that is in the heavens and the earth glorifieth Him, and He is the Mighty, the Wise

3s3ztIlq1Fg.speaker_note: Friday Arabic tafsir series on Surah Ya-Sin, continuing from the previous week in his usual format
3s3ztIlq1Fg.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surah Ya-Sin (36:33-40)
3s3ztIlq1Fg.one_line: The signs of the revived earth, night and day, sun and moon in Ya-Sin, read as lessons on reviving the dead soul and knowing Allah.
3s3ztIlq1Fg.summary: He frames Surah Ya-Sin as a surah about life and death, where real life is the life of the soul through obedience, concern for the religion and calling to Allah, and where many people breathe while their souls have died. After the story of the believer of Ya-Sin, the surah turns to the universe, as Makki surahs always do: faith is reached by looking at creation, and the Quran then teaches rulings and deepens that faith. The dead earth brought back to life is a picture of the dead soul that only Allah revives, and recognising that He gave the life is itself a form of life. He prefers reading the phrase about what their hands made as a negation, which leads into gratitude and an attack on the inflated ego of Muslims today. Explaining subhan, he describes it as declaring Allah beyond blame or question, and contrasts it with how other faiths speak of God. He then lays out four ways to know Allah: the unified laws of the cosmos, the mystery of life, the history of revelation to every nation, and the inner witness of the self. The night, the sun's course, the moon's phases and the orbits close the passage, each doing the task assigned to it.

outline.heading: Why people love Ya-Sin
outline.gist: Ya-Sin is among the surahs people memorise and recite most, and they love it for good reasons.

outline.heading: The surah's axis: life and death of the soul
outline.gist: Life is not only breath and biology; the soul lives by obedience and calling to Allah and dies when starved of Him.

outline.heading: Recap: heedlessness and the believer of Ya-Sin
outline.gist: The earlier passages described the heedless, and the believer of Ya-Sin leaves no believer an excuse for not calling to Allah.

outline.heading: Makki surahs turn you to the universe
outline.gist: Faith is reached by reading the page of creation; the Quran then gives rulings and strengthens the faith of one who already follows the reminder.

outline.heading: Three signs, each opening with 'a sign for them'
outline.gist: He recites the passage and shows it is built of three small sections, each starting with the same phrase.

outline.heading: The dead earth revived: the dead soul revived
outline.gist: Right after the story, the surah speaks of reviving dead earth; a soul that feels nothing at the Quran can likewise be brought to life by Allah.

outline.heading: Gardens, springs and the dispute over 'what their hands made'
outline.gist: He presents the two readings of the particle, relative or negating, and prefers the negation while accepting both meanings.

outline.heading: The seed looks dead: we only plant
outline.gist: People place seeds and water them, but cannot make anything grow; the first steps of life are given, not made, so they should give thanks.

outline.heading: Mayta and mayyit: dead now versus destined to die
outline.gist: The word used for the earth means it is lifeless now, unlike the word for one who will die later.

outline.heading: A revived soul yields gardens and springs of knowledge
outline.gist: When Allah revives a soul He brings out abundant good from it that benefits many people, and none of it is the person's own work.

outline.heading: Recognising the Giver is itself life
outline.gist: As long as one thinks he achieved things himself he remains dead; we are a nation of praise that credits Allah, not ourselves.

outline.heading: The inflated ego of Muslims today
outline.gist: Muslims' core problem is unpurified, swollen selves; the whole universe cannot hold their heads, and they need souls that know Allah gave them everything.

outline.heading: Only Allah gives life: reform starts with yourself
outline.gist: He alone revives earth and soul, so a person walking around proud of himself must begin reform with his own self.

outline.heading: The meaning of subhan
outline.gist: Saying subhan declares that the One named is beyond blame, error or questioning; any discomfort comes from the self's shortcomings.

outline.heading: Tasbih: what separates the Muslim's speech about God
outline.gist: He is not asked about what He does; from his conversations with clergy he notes that other faiths describe God in ways a Muslim cannot accept.

outline.heading: Pairs from the earth, from ourselves, and the unknown
outline.gist: There are pairs we cannot see or grasp; our whole observable universe may be a small part of what Allah created.

outline.heading: What an ayah is: a sign pointing to Allah
outline.gist: The verse of glorification sits between the three signs; an ayah is that which points to something else, and the Prophet taught people Allah through the signs of the cosmos.

outline.heading: The maker is known by the work
outline.gist: As a carpenter is judged by his chair, Allah is known from the precision of what He made.

outline.heading: First station: one set of laws across the cosmos
outline.gist: From atom to galaxy everything spins the same way, as pilgrims do in tawaf, and the same elements and laws everywhere point to one Maker.

outline.heading: Second station: where did life come from
outline.gist: The first living compound that wanted to live, adapted and survived repeated mass extinctions raises the question of who programmed it.

outline.heading: The moth that eats for six weeks and has no mouth
outline.gist: He describes a giant moth whose wings mimic a cobra and which lives a week only to mate, as an example of purposeful design.

outline.heading: Evolution deepens tasbih
outline.gist: Even if life unfolded from one first cell and one genetic code, that only increases his amazement and glorification.

outline.heading: Third station: history and revelation to every nation
outline.gist: Allah has kept sending messengers; every civilization has a temple, even when people later distorted the message or killed their prophets.

outline.heading: Shared moral core across religions; marriage
outline.gist: Despite creedal distortion, faiths agree on forbidding adultery, wine, killing and theft, and every nation has marriage, which humans would not have invented.

outline.heading: Fourth station: the witness inside the self
outline.gist: Everyone knows within that someone watches over them and helped them along; this is the strongest argument against a person on the Day of Judgment.

outline.heading: Then the Quran: knowing His will and returning to Him
outline.gist: Once a person knows Allah through these stations, he reads His book to learn His names and what He wants, and takes the road back to Him.

outline.heading: Recitation of the night, sun, moon and orbit verses
outline.gist: He recites the verses on night, the sun, the moon and the orbits.

outline.heading: Earth, night, ships: the joints of our existence
outline.gist: The three successive signs name the basic frames of human life: land, the motion of the heavens, and provision.

outline.heading: Night stripped of day: darkness is the larger reality
outline.gist: The day is peeled off a part of the night; outside the earth the universe is utter darkness.

outline.heading: What life would be without the day
outline.gist: Long polar nights bring depression and high suicide, and constant light is used as torture; the alternation is a mercy.

outline.heading: The sun runs to its resting place
outline.gist: Its resting place is beneath the Throne; every heavenly body has an end appointed from its creation, as a person does.

outline.heading: The decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing
outline.gist: Al-Aziz is beyond reach and questioning; paired with Al-Alim, His unquestioned power never errs because nothing escapes His knowledge.

outline.heading: The moon's stations and the old palm stalk
outline.gist: He explains the urjun, the dried bent date stalk, and how the moon's phases let people tell the date and count days of travel.

outline.heading: The sun may not overtake the moon
outline.gist: Overtaking here means collision; each body does the task Allah assigned without encroaching on the other.

outline.heading: Nor does night outstrip the day
outline.gist: Sabiq here means overpowering, not coming first in time, and he supports this with a line of classical poetry.

outline.heading: Each swims in an orbit
outline.gist: Falak implies a path that is not a perfect circle; sun, moon, night and day each move in their course as commanded.

outline.heading: Outro

quran.point: The Quran benefits one who already follows the reminder and fears the Most Merciful unseen.
Example of mayyit: one who will die later, contrasted with the earth that is dead now.
He is not asked about what He does, while they are asked: the core of tasbih.
Nothing is like Him, the standard for how a Muslim speaks about God.
Horses, mules and donkeys, and He creates what you do not know: parallel to pairs we do not know.
Ibrahim's prayer for a messenger reciting Allah's signs, used to show ayat can mean signs in creation.
Reciting the signs is listed separately from teaching the Book, so the signs are those of the universe.
Return the gaze and see no flaw: look at the cosmos as one coherent order.
Every nation had a warner: Allah has addressed humanity throughout history.
Whoever wills takes a path to his Lord: knowing Allah means returning to Him.
The sun will be wrapped up: its course has an appointed end.
The Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner: the only answer to how Allah is.

takeaways: Check whether your soul is alive: does the Quran move you, and do you feel attachment to Allah?
Credit every achievement to Allah and praise Him rather than yourself.

Say subhan Allah with awareness that He is beyond blame or question.

36:41.ar: وَءَايَةࣱ لَّهُمۡ أَنَّا حَمَلۡنَا ذُرِّيَّتَهُمۡ فِي ٱلۡفُلۡكِ ٱلۡمَشۡحُونِ
36:41.en: And a token unto them is that We bear their offspring in the laden ship

36:42.ar: وَخَلَقۡنَا لَهُم مِّن مِّثۡلِهِۦ مَا يَرۡكَبُونَ
36:42.en: And have created for them of the like thereof whereon they ride

36:43.ar: وَإِن نَّشَأۡ نُغۡرِقۡهُمۡ فَلَا صَرِيخَ لَهُمۡ وَلَا هُمۡ يُنقَذُونَ
36:43.en: And if We will, We drown them, and there is no help for them, neither can they be saved

36:44.ar: إِلَّا رَحۡمَةࣰ مِّنَّا وَمَتَٰعًا إِلَىٰ حِينࣲ‏
36:44.en: Unless by mercy from Us and as comfort for a while

36:45.ar: وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمُ ٱتَّقُواْ مَا بَيۡنَ أَيۡدِيكُمۡ وَمَا خَلۡفَكُمۡ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تُرۡحَمُونَ
36:45.en: When it is said unto them: Beware of that which is before you and that which is behind you, that haply ye may find mercy (they are heedless)

36:46.ar: وَمَا تَأۡتِيهِم مِّنۡ ءَايَةࣲ مِّنۡ ءَايَٰتِ رَبِّهِمۡ إِلَّا كَانُواْ عَنۡهَا مُعۡرِضِينَ
36:46.en: Never came a token of the tokens of their Lord to them, but they did turn away from it

36:47.ar: وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمۡ أَنفِقُواْ مِمَّا رَزَقَكُمُ ٱللَّهُ قَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ لِلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ أَنُطۡعِمُ مَن لَّوۡ يَشَآءُ ٱللَّهُ أَطۡعَمَهُۥٓ إِنۡ أَنتُمۡ إِلَّا فِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينࣲ‏
36:47.en: And when it is said unto them: Spend of that wherewith Allah hath provided you, those who disbelieve say unto those who believe: Shall we feed those whom Allah, if He willed, would feed? Ye are in naught else than error manifest

36:40.ar: لَا ٱلشَّمۡسُ يَنۢبَغِي لَهَآ أَن تُدۡرِكَ ٱلۡقَمَرَ وَلَا ٱلَّيۡلُ سَابِقُ ٱلنَّهَارِۚ وَكُلࣱّ فِي فَلَكࣲ يَسۡبَحُونَ
36:40.en: It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor doth the night outstrip the day. They float each in an orbit

45:28.ar: وَتَرَىٰ كُلَّ أُمَّةࣲ جَاثِيَةࣰۚ كُلُّ أُمَّةࣲ تُدۡعَىٰٓ إِلَىٰ كِتَٰبِهَا ٱلۡيَوۡمَ تُجۡزَوۡنَ مَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
45:28.en: And thou wilt see each nation crouching, each nation summoned to its record. (And it will be said unto them): This day ye are requited what ye used to do

YbIPBAxgTIg.speaker: adnan
YbIPBAxgTIg.speaker_note: Friday Arabic tafsir series on Surah Ya-Sin, continuing from the previous week
YbIPBAxgTIg.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surah Ya-Sin (36:41-47)
YbIPBAxgTIg.one_line: The sign of the laden ship, Noah's foresight, and why dead souls ignore signs and refuse to give: Ya-Sin as a call to play your role.
YbIPBAxgTIg.summary: He places Ya-Sin in a group of surahs from Al-Ahzab to Az-Zumar about obedience and submission, each from a different angle: obedience under hardship, the obedience of whole societies, obedience grounded in understanding, and in Ya-Sin obedience that includes wanting others to obey Allah. Without that concern for others, a person is alive in body but dead in soul. The sun, moon, night and day each keep to their task, and the question for us is whether we know and fulfil our own role. He argues that no Muslim may withdraw from people except under persecution, that all humanity is the Prophet's nation to be invited, and that most invitation happens through character, competence and strength rather than sermons or online channels. The laden ship recalls Noah building an ark on a mountain, mocked for preparing for what no one else could see; the believer prepares the same way for the Day of Judgment. Allah could drown us at any moment, which exposes human weakness. People surrounded by signs stop seeing them through familiarity, and a dead soul refuses to spend, asking why it should feed someone Allah could feed. He urges giving from whatever one has been given.

outline.heading: Ya-Sin in the axis of obedience and submission
outline.gist: Ya-Sin is among the surahs from Al-Ahzab to Az-Zumar that treat obedience to Allah, the greatest issue in the religion, from several angles.

outline.heading: Al-Ahzab: obeying when it is hard
outline.gist: A topic as large as obedience cannot be summed up in a sentence; Al-Ahzab treats obedience under difficulty and strain.

outline.heading: Saba: the obedience of societies
outline.gist: Nations obey or disobey collectively; communal obligations left undone make the whole community accountable, each by his position and means.

outline.heading: Fatir: obeying with understanding
outline.gist: Allah must be obeyed as He wants, which requires knowledge and a sound grasp of what He intends.

outline.heading: Ya-Sin: obedience that loves others to obey
outline.gist: Obedience is incomplete until one wants others to obey and enjoy Allah too, not because He needs it but out of love for Him.

outline.heading: Reading Ya-Sin over the dead: death of the soul
outline.gist: The custom of reading it for the dead is widespread and fine, but the death the surah addresses is the soul's death through heedlessness.

outline.heading: Recap: the believer of Ya-Sin
outline.gist: An outsider to a foolish people with three prophets among them still came running to advise them, was killed, and wished they knew his reward.

outline.heading: Recap: the revived earth and revived soul
outline.gist: As Allah revives dead earth and brings out food and gardens, He revives a dried-up soul and brings out good for everyone.

outline.heading: Sun, moon, night and day each keep their task
outline.gist: Overtaking means encroaching; no body tries to take another's role, and each swims in its own orbit.

outline.heading: Has the human grasped his role?
outline.gist: The believer of Ya-Sin had no customary duty to act, yet he did not stay home minding only his family.

outline.heading: No staying home except under persecution
outline.gist: Withdrawal is allowed only when one is forced out or denied religious freedom; otherwise a Muslim must mix with, learn from, teach and serve people.

outline.heading: All humanity is the Prophet's nation
outline.gist: There is the nation that answered and the nation still to be invited; everyone on earth belongs to his call.

outline.heading: The exception for the oppressed and emigration
outline.gist: The permission to leave a land of oppression is a mercy, yet the standard of the believer of Ya-Sin remains.

outline.heading: Most invitation is by conduct, not pulpits
outline.gist: The role of speakers is small and overrated, limited to clarifying basics and boundaries; real invitation comes through mixing, good character and work.

outline.heading: Build strength, as the Prophet built a core
outline.gist: Not everyone should open a YouTube channel; Muslims need economic, social, political and academic strength so their character is seen.

outline.heading: Do your role or be a burden
outline.gist: The sun never takes a day off; if we do not fulfil our role, our existence is a burden and we will be held to account.

outline.heading: Recitation of the third sign
outline.gist: He recites the verses on the laden ship.

outline.heading: Grammar of 'if We will, We drown them'
outline.gist: The conditional makes both verbs jussive, so the hamzah and the qaf are read with sukun.

outline.heading: The first two signs applied to us
outline.gist: Before Ramadan everyone's heart battery is flashing, and Allah recharges it; like the heavenly bodies, each of us has an orbit to keep.

outline.heading: The laden ship: Noah's ark carrying our ancestors
outline.gist: The verse recalls the blessing on Noah, whose full ark carried the offspring of humanity.

outline.heading: Building a ship on a mountain
outline.gist: Noah built far from any body of water, which would seem absurd to any observer.

outline.heading: Humans cannot plan beyond what they see
outline.gist: Our inability to prepare for an unseen future is why we have damaged the planet, ignoring warnings about burning fuel and melting poles.

outline.heading: Mocked for preparing; the flood proves him wise
outline.gist: His people jeered that the prophet had become a carpenter; when the water rose above the mountains, he was the sanest one there.

outline.heading: The believer prepares for the Day of Judgment
outline.gist: The greatest future to prepare for is the Hour; short-sighted people mock the one who invests in it instead of wealth and status.

outline.heading: Calling to Allah is never paid
outline.gist: The prophets asked no wage; those who seek gain from it have made it a trade, and students often forget or turn on their teachers.

outline.heading: The believer of Ya-Sin's sincerity
outline.gist: Killed while young for caring about his people, he still wished them well, and urged them to follow those who ask no wage.

outline.heading: We taught you ships and made similar mounts
outline.gist: Had Allah not taught people to build and plan, they would all have drowned; He also filled land and sea with means of travel.

outline.heading: No one to cry out to
outline.gist: With all our preparation, Allah could drown us; the sarikh is the one called on for rescue, and wood floats only by laws He set.

outline.heading: Mercy and enjoyment for a time: human weakness
outline.gist: We merely learned how things work and cannot force anything; all that remains is to learn our role and fulfil it.

outline.heading: No one can foresee the end of the world
outline.gist: Who would expect the earth to stop turning or the sun to rise in the west? Allah has told us it will happen, and only the prepared will cope.

outline.heading: Until that time comes
outline.gist: Ships float and seeds grow by mercy until the appointed time, when the laws stop and only the one who prepared is saved.

outline.heading: Recitation of the closing verses
outline.gist: He recites the verses on their turning away and their refusal to spend.

outline.heading: The passage ends with an example
outline.gist: After pointing us to the universe and past nations, Allah gives examples of how the heedless respond.

outline.heading: Fear what is before you and behind you
outline.gist: The past is guarded against by seeking forgiveness and repentance, the future by planning and changing direction, including making invitation part of daily life.

outline.heading: The omitted answer: they turned away
outline.gist: The response is left out because it is clear from the next verse, which states it.

outline.heading: Which signs came to them?
outline.gist: The earth, the night and the ship: Allah surrounds us with signs at every moment, with no need for the sea to split.

outline.heading: Familiarity makes us blind to signs
outline.gist: What we see daily loses its wonder, as the proverb says to visit rarely to be loved more.

outline.heading: Colour-blind people seeing colour for the first time
outline.gist: Videos of them weeping at red and blue show the wonder we have stopped noticing.

outline.heading: Complaining about rain
outline.gist: Arriving from a drought in Syria, he was struck that people here grumbled about rain, a gift from the sky.

outline.heading: Asking for signs while ignoring them
outline.gist: People demand a sign, though they would not believe if it came, because they see signs and refuse to look.

outline.heading: A living soul sees Allah everywhere
outline.gist: A living soul becomes sensitive and sees Allah in creation, death and beauty, even in ugliness; a dead soul would not believe if it saw Him.

outline.heading: Dead souls refuse to call others
outline.gist: Asked to invite people, they say it is not their business, misusing the verse about guarding oneself, which Abu Bakr corrected.

outline.heading: 'Shall we feed one whom Allah could feed?'
outline.gist: The disbelievers accuse the believers of error for asking them to give; concepts become completely confused.

outline.heading: Spend from whatever you have been given
outline.gist: Spending can be knowledge, time, tolerance or a listening ear; Allah gave you so that you give, and life is designed around that flow.

outline.heading: Outro

IYVwAwKRvlU.title: The Battle of Mu'tah
IYVwAwKRvlU.one_line: The Battle of Mu'tah: three martyred commanders, Khalid's tactical retreat, lessons on hesitation, merit over seniority and ambition, then the setting of Khaybar.
IYVwAwKRvlU.summary: After Hudaybiyyah the Prophet's outreach widened, and when a Ghassanid ruler killed his envoy he sent an army of three thousand to show that every Muslim, however unknown, mattered. The sheikh narrates Mu'tah: the consultation, Abdullah ibn Rawaha's speech, the Romans targeting the banner, and the martyrdom of Zayd, Ja'far and Abdullah, which the Prophet described live from Madinah. He pauses on the Prophet's lifetime of bereavement and how he kept moving forward. Ibn Rawaha's brief hesitation leads to a pointed question: how many moments of hesitation will we regret? When Thabit hands the banner to the newly converted Khalid, he draws a lesson for the community: put the most qualified person in place, not the oldest or best connected, and keep ego out. He then describes Khalid's deception that let the army withdraw, the 'Sword of Allah' title, and the idea that latecomers can make up ground by working harder. He urges young people to build strength of every kind, to aim embarrassingly high, and asks elders to believe in the young. He closes by introducing Khaybar, its castles and its role in the conspiracies against Madinah, and the story of a twelve-year-old girl the Prophet honoured.

outline.heading: After Hudaybiyyah: dawah to kings and tribes
outline.gist: The truce let the Prophet send letters to rulers, and whole tribes began entering Islam.

outline.heading: The envoy murdered: every Muslim is worth an army
outline.gist: A Ghassanid ruler kills the Prophet's messenger; the Prophet mobilises for an almost unknown companion, teaching that every citizen matters and giving people ownership of the deen.

outline.heading: Three thousand against a vast army: the consultation
outline.gist: Zayd, Ja'far and Abdullah are named in order; facing a huge Roman-Arab force, the commanders consult on retreating, waiting for help or pressing on.

outline.heading: Ibn Rawaha's speech and the stand at Mu'tah
outline.gist: Abdullah ibn Rawaha reminds them they came seeking martyrdom; they choose the town of Mu'tah, whose masjid still stands in Jordan.

outline.heading: Day seven: the Romans target the banner, Zayd falls
outline.gist: After six good days the Romans aim at the standard-bearer; Zayd is killed and the Prophet narrates it live from the minbar.

outline.heading: The Prophet's many bereavements and his resilience
outline.gist: He lost over eighteen close relatives yet kept smiling and moving forward, through trust in Allah and a realistic expectation of life.

outline.heading: Ja'far's martyrdom and his two wings
outline.gist: Ja'far holds the banner after losing both arms, all wounds in front; the Prophet sees him in Paradise with two wings, a month after his return from Abyssinia.

outline.heading: Ibn Rawaha's hesitation: how many moments have we hesitated?
outline.gist: His brief hesitation placed him a little lower in Paradise; the sheikh asks the audience to prepare so they act without hesitation when the moment comes.

outline.heading: Thabit and being the person everyone wants on the team
outline.gist: Being valued on a team in life comes from skill, dedication, humility and commitment, not physical gifts.

outline.heading: Khalid takes the banner: his genius and humility
outline.gist: Khalid's brilliance spawned myths, Umar demoted him, and he served on without complaint; the story from Yarmuk shows his reputation.

outline.heading: Qualification over seniority; ego blinds
outline.gist: The companions chose the most qualified, not the most senior; communities stall when ego and control keep the right person out; the Prophet let Khalid earn his place by merit.

outline.heading: Khalid's assessment: a strategic withdrawal
outline.gist: With the point made and victory impossible, Khalid proposes a retreat but knows open flight would be fatal.

outline.heading: Khalid's ruse: dust, fresh banners and cavalry waves
outline.gist: Rotating flanks, new clothes, dust on the horizon and six cavalry charges convince the Romans reinforcements have come; the Muslims slip away to Madinah.

outline.heading: The return: 'runaways' and the Sword of Allah
outline.gist: Madinah's women shame the army for retreating, showing how the community valued standing firm; the Prophet defends them and names Khalid a sword of Allah.

outline.heading: Khalid's death in bed
outline.gist: Khalid wept at dying at home; the sheikh reflects that a sword of Allah would not be broken in battle.

outline.heading: Coming late, pushing harder
outline.gist: Late converts like Khalid made up for lost time by going the extra mile; it is never too late to start.

outline.heading: The strong believer: building every kind of strength
outline.gist: The hadith of the strong believer covers intellectual, social, academic and financial strength, all earned by hard work.

outline.heading: Ambition: aim embarrassingly high
outline.gist: He finds ambition harder to inspire in Canada than in the Middle East; the trench prophecy shows ambition beyond circumstance, and belief in Allah implies belief in yourself.

outline.heading: One generation can turn it around
outline.gist: The Prophet raised one generation that toppled empires after him; elders should believe in the young as he believed in his companions.

outline.heading: When was Khaybar? A dating disagreement
outline.gist: Seerah scholars differ on Khaybar's timing; he places it after Mu'tah and notes the disagreement does not change the story.

outline.heading: Khaybar: wealth, eight castles and a hub of conspiracy
outline.gist: Khaybar's palms, ten thousand warriors and fortresses made it impregnable, and the exiled tribes there funded raids and the Confederate army.

outline.heading: Neutralising Khaybar by forcing a treaty
outline.gist: Repeated attempts at treaties failed, so the Prophet moved to neutralise the threat, ending in terms rather than a full war.

outline.heading: The army of 1400 and the growing role of women
outline.gist: Women's participation rose with each campaign, in real roles such as Rufaydah's medical unit, unlike the Arab practice of bringing women only to stop men fleeing.

outline.heading: The twelve-year-old girl who joined the army
outline.gist: The Prophet kept a girl who came alone with him, placed her with the medics and gave her a necklace from the spoils, nurturing her spirit instead of sending her home.

outline.heading: Outro

gOG8V7z3RDg.title: Perspective on the Earthquake in Turkiye and Syria
gOG8V7z3RDg.one_line: Responding to the 2023 Turkiye-Syria earthquake: never call others' disasters punishment for their sins; treat it as a shared test and help.
gOG8V7z3RDg.summary: Speaking after the February 2023 earthquake in Turkiye and Syria, he first apologizes that disasters in some parts of the world go unnoticed, insisting no human life is worth less than another. What troubles him most is not the images but the comments claiming the victims were punished for their sins. Catastrophes are part of the deal of living on this planet, as earth's long history shows, and they are a test for everyone: for those under the rubble and equally for those watching. Calling an event a punishment requires direct word from Allah; the Quran names specific punishments such as the people of Lut, but no one else has that right. Saying it from the comfort of one's home is arrogance, and needing an earthquake to feel weak is itself a sign of arrogance. The proper response is to recognise that we belong to one ummah and one humanity and to respond emotionally, intellectually, financially and socially, quietly doing the work even one person at a time; if every masjid helped one person, much suffering would be relieved. Thinking it could not happen to us is an escape from reality. He asks people to be grateful, humble, make dua for the victims and support relief efforts.

outline.heading: Addressing the earthquake and unnoticed disasters
outline.gist: He finds it hard to speak about such tragedies and apologizes that disasters in some regions go unnoticed.

outline.heading: Disasters are part of the deal of life on earth
outline.gist: The planet has seen mass extinctions; being alive with a mind and soul comes with pain and catastrophe.

outline.heading: A test for those under the rubble and those watching
outline.gist: People blaming the victims' sins have no basis; the event is a test for all, equally.

outline.heading: Calling it punishment requires word from Allah
outline.gist: Unless Allah told you directly, hold your tongue; saying it from comfort is arrogance, and needing an earthquake to feel weak is arrogance too.

outline.heading: We belong to one ummah and one humanity
outline.gist: Such events should remind us we are part of a bigger human whole, so we respond emotionally, intellectually, financially and socially.

outline.heading: Do the work, one person at a time
outline.gist: Instead of objecting to the sky, quietly relieve suffering; if every masjid helped one person the need would shrink. Give what you can and let it make you more thankful.

outline.heading: The tsunami and the Quran's named punishments
outline.gist: The same claims followed an earlier tsunami; the Quran names punishments like that of Lut's people, but we have no right to label others' calamities.

outline.heading: It could happen to any of us
outline.gist: Blaming victims is a cowardly escape from the reality that no one is immune.

outline.heading: Humility, dua and support
outline.gist: If Allah kept you safe, respond humbly with reverence, keep the victims in your dua and support relief efforts.

RvUX9v2ZuvE.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Waqi'ah, Part 3: Verses 41-56
RvUX9v2ZuvE.one_line: Al-Waqi'ah 41-56: aim high, the people of the left, why just punishment exists, luxury and denial of accountability, and the Fire paraded.
RvUX9v2ZuvE.summary: He recommends memorising the surahs from Qaf to Al-Hadid and recaps their chain of choices leading to the three groups. Fewer forerunners come from later generations because gratitude amid abundance is harder than patience in hunger, as companions who tied stones to their stomachs still lamented their later ease. He insists that aiming merely to squeeze into Paradise is disrespectful when Allah offers Firdaws, and warns that we remain Muslim only because Allah has not exploited our weaknesses. The people of the left face scorching wind, boiling water and a shade of black smoke. Fire also cleanses, and just punishment is necessary: without it tyrants escape, and without opposites humans cannot understand good. Allah owes us nothing, owns us and cannot oppress us, yet human arrogance questions Him. The cause given is excessive luxury that led to persisting in shirk and denying resurrection. Wealth is not the problem; the question is whether you own it or it owns you. Denying resurrection is denying accountability, and believers whose conduct ignores it are in a dangerous grey area, since tawhid should fix one's moral lines. He distinguishes kufr from knowing denial, warns that the believers' real risk is drifting into being lost, and describes zaqqum and the Fire paraded before kneeling nations as a warning given out of mercy.

outline.heading: Memorise the surahs from Qaf to Al-Hadid
outline.gist: If you cannot memorise the whole Quran, this cluster summarises its values and principles.

outline.heading: The cluster's chain of choices
outline.gist: Righteousness or falsehood, purpose, guidance, certainty, using and thanking for blessings, and finally which of three groups you will be.

outline.heading: Worldly groupings are thrown away
outline.gist: The circles we form by status, education, colour, language and income are burned; only three groups remain.

outline.heading: Your values and deeds decide your group
outline.gist: What you stood for and did with your time, knowledge and wealth; the Day brings surprise, joy and confusion.

outline.heading: The forerunners soared
outline.gist: Not up one day and down the next; they were clear, emotionally attached to the message and moved as fast as they could.

outline.heading: Fewer forerunners among later generations
outline.gist: Patience in hardship comes more steadily than gratitude for far more than we need, and recent generations live in unprecedented comfort.

outline.heading: Companions who tied stones to their stomachs
outline.gist: They missed the hungry days because they knew who they were then, and feared even modest ease broke their covenant.

outline.heading: Accountability for what you consume
outline.gist: You may buy a nice car and home, but the more you are given the more you answer for its use.

outline.heading: Aiming low is disrespectful
outline.gist: The people of the right are equal across generations, but settling for being pushed through the door while wanting the best of this world is rude to the One offering eternity.

outline.heading: Ask for the highest Paradise; drop the word 'deserve'
outline.gist: No one deserves anything, so deserving is not the question; refusing to aim high says you do not want what He offers.

outline.heading: Allah looks at your intentions
outline.gist: Those who aimed high and fell short differ from those with no ambition, because Allah judges the heart.

outline.heading: Muslim only because our weakness was not exploited
outline.gist: Allah told the believers at the Trench that many would have abandoned their faith had the enemy entered; know your own weakness and fortify it.

outline.heading: Reciting the passage on the people of the left
outline.gist: Heavy verses most of us prefer not to think about, but they motivate.

outline.heading: Scorching wind, boiling water, a shade of black smoke
outline.gist: Yahmum is smoke so thick it casts a shadow, a shade that is neither cool nor refreshing.

outline.heading: Fire as cleansing
outline.gist: Like a fever burning out an intruder, the Fire carries both punishment and purification.

outline.heading: Why just punishment must exist
outline.gist: Imagine those who killed millions getting away with it with nothing afterward; our opinion on who deserves the Fire was never asked.

outline.heading: Nothing is understood without its opposite
outline.gist: Pleasure has meaning only against pain, and science itself advances by comparing outcomes.

outline.heading: Children who never saw a bad day
outline.gist: They cannot appreciate what they have, so parents should let them see hardship in controlled ways; near-death survivors appreciate everything.

outline.heading: Punishment shows that deeds matter
outline.gist: It teaches that we are accountable and that refusing basic commands after being given everything is justly punished.

outline.heading: What does Allah owe us?
outline.gist: To be owed you need rights, and we have none beyond what He chose to give; He promises never to wrong anyone, so worry about yourself.

outline.heading: He owns us; human arrogance has no limit
outline.gist: One cannot oppress one's own property, yet having refused eternal bliss we still ask why He would punish.

outline.heading: Some take long to cleanse
outline.gist: For some the cleansing takes very long, and some may have taken on something almost unfixable.

outline.heading: They lived in excessive luxury
outline.gist: Only for this group does the surah give a cause: they had far more than they needed and did not use it as they should.

outline.heading: Do you own your wealth or does it own you?
outline.gist: Having wealth is not wrong; become the richest person if you can, then use it as it should be used.

outline.heading: Persisting in the great sin
outline.gist: Hinth is a false oath; the great falsehood is shirk, and they mocked the resurrection of dust and bones.

outline.heading: Restored down to the fingerprints
outline.gist: After years in the grave nothing remains, yet Allah will bring people back exactly as they were.

outline.heading: Denying resurrection is denying accountability
outline.gist: Belief in resurrection should be the first thought before every decision; without it there is no reason to care for others or for justice.

outline.heading: Believers who live as if there is no reckoning
outline.gist: Some who deny the afterlife act with care for others while some believers cheat and harm, making belief a cultural slogan.

outline.heading: Belief must show in conduct
outline.gist: Allah treats belief and action as one; saying one thing and doing the opposite with no remorse is a form of hypocrisy.

outline.heading: Tawhid fixes the lines
outline.gist: Shirk is named because tawhid is the most consequential belief: lines drawn by the Divine do not move with time, place or temptation.

outline.heading: The grey area between belief and conduct

outline.heading: All gathered on an appointed day
outline.gist: First and last are gathered at one moment and judged swiftly; worry only about what is in your book and how you will defend it.

outline.heading: Six-count madd and recitation
outline.gist: A madd followed by a shaddah is always six counts.

outline.heading: The lost and the deniers
outline.gist: Kufr is any disbelief; takdhib is rejecting what made sense to you for personal reasons.

outline.heading: Being lost is the believers' real risk

outline.heading: Zaqqum and drinking like thirsty camels
outline.gist: They fill their bellies with what does not nourish and drink boiling water that does not quench.

outline.heading: Their accommodation on the Day

outline.heading: Why Allah warns us of punishment

outline.heading: The Fire paraded before kneeling nations

2:143.ar: وَكَذَٰلِكَ جَعَلۡنَٰكُمۡ أُمَّةࣰ وَسَطࣰ ا لِّتَكُونُواْ شُهَدَآءَ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ وَيَكُونَ ٱلرَّسُولُ عَلَيۡكُمۡ شَهِيدࣰ اۗ وَمَا جَعَلۡنَا ٱلۡقِبۡلَةَ ٱلَّتِي كُنتَ عَلَيۡهَآ إِلَّا لِنَعۡلَمَ مَن يَتَّبِعُ ٱلرَّسُولَ مِمَّن يَنقَلِبُ عَلَىٰ عَقِبَيۡهِۚ وَإِن كَانَتۡ لَكَبِيرَةً إِلَّا عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ هَدَى ٱللَّهُۗ وَمَا كَانَ ٱللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إِيمَٰنَكُمۡۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِٱلنَّاسِ لَرَءُوفࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
2:143.en: Thus We have appointed you a middle nation, that ye may be witnesses against mankind, and that the messenger may be a witness against you. And We appointed the qiblah which ye formerly observed only that We might know him who followeth the messenger, from him who turneth on his heels. In truth it was a hard (test) save for those whom Allah guided. But it was not Allah's purpose that your faith should be in vain, for Allah is Full of Pity, Merciful toward mankind

16:116.ar: وَلَا تَقُولُواْ لِمَا تَصِفُ أَلۡسِنَتُكُمُ ٱلۡكَذِبَ هَٰذَا حَلَٰلࣱ وَهَٰذَا حَرَامࣱ لِّتَفۡتَرُواْ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ ٱلۡكَذِبَۚ إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ يَفۡتَرُونَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ ٱلۡكَذِبَ لَا يُفۡلِحُونَ
16:116.en: And speak not, concerning that which your own tongues qualify (as clean or unclean), the falsehood: "This is lawful, and this is forbidden," so that ye invent a lie against Allah. Lo! those who invent a lie against Allah will not succeed

16:117.en: A brief enjoyment (will be theirs); and theirs a painful doom

10:59.ar: قُلۡ أَرَءَيۡتُم مَّآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ لَكُم مِّن رِّزۡقࣲ فَجَعَلۡتُم مِّنۡهُ حَرَامࣰ ا وَحَلَٰلࣰ ا قُلۡ ءَآللَّهُ أَذِنَ لَكُمۡۖ أَمۡ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ تَفۡتَرُونَ

10:60.ar: وَمَا ظَنُّ ٱلَّذِينَ يَفۡتَرُونَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ ٱلۡكَذِبَ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَذُو فَضۡلٍ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَهُمۡ لَا يَشۡكُرُونَ

65:1.en: O Prophet! When ye (men) put away women, put them away for their (legal) period and reckon the period, and keep your duty to Allah, your Lord. Expel them not from their houses nor let them go forth unless they commit open immorality. Such are the limits (imposed by) Allah; and whoso transgresseth Allah's limits, he verily wrongeth his soul. Thou knowest not: it may be that Allah will afterward bring some new thing to pass

4:14.ar: وَمَن يَعۡصِ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥ وَيَتَعَدَّ حُدُودَهُۥ يُدۡخِلۡهُ نَارًا خَٰلِدࣰ ا فِيهَا وَلَهُۥ عَذَابࣱ مُّهِينࣱ‏
4:14.en: And whoso disobeyeth Allah and His messenger and transgresseth His limits, He will make him enter Fire, where he will dwell for ever; his will be a shameful doom

2:275.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ يَأۡكُلُونَ ٱلرِّبَوٰاْ لَا يَقُومُونَ إِلَّا كَمَا يَقُومُ ٱلَّذِي يَتَخَبَّطُهُ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنُ مِنَ ٱلۡمَسِّۚ ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمۡ قَالُوٓاْ إِنَّمَا ٱلۡبَيۡعُ مِثۡلُ ٱلرِّبَوٰاْۗ وَأَحَلَّ ٱللَّهُ ٱلۡبَيۡعَ وَحَرَّمَ ٱلرِّبَوٰاْۚ فَمَن جَآءَهُۥ مَوۡعِظَةࣱ مِّن رَّبِّهِۦ فَٱنتَهَىٰ فَلَهُۥ مَا سَلَفَ وَأَمۡرُهُۥٓ إِلَى ٱللَّهِۖ وَمَنۡ عَادَ فَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ أَصۡحَٰبُ ٱلنَّارِۖ هُمۡ فِيهَا خَٰلِدُونَ
2:275.en: Those who swallow usury cannot rise up save as he ariseth whom the devil hath prostrated by (his) touch. That is because they say: Trade is just like usury; whereas Allah permitteth trading and forbiddeth usury. He unto whom an admonition from his Lord cometh, and (he) refraineth (in obedience thereto), he shall keep (the profits of) that which is past, and his affair (henceforth) is with Allah. As for him who returneth (to usury) - Such are rightful owners of the Fire. They will abide therein

9:37.ar: إِنَّمَا ٱلنَّسِيٓءُ زِيَادَةࣱ فِي ٱلۡكُفۡرِۖ يُضَلُّ بِهِ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ يُحِلُّونَهُۥ عَامࣰ ا وَيُحَرِّمُونَهُۥ عَامࣰ ا لِّيُوَاطِـُٔواْ عِدَّةَ مَا حَرَّمَ ٱللَّهُ فَيُحِلُّواْ مَا حَرَّمَ ٱللَّهُۚ زُيِّنَ لَهُمۡ سُوٓءُ أَعۡمَٰلِهِمۡۗ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَهۡدِي ٱلۡقَوۡمَ ٱلۡكَٰفِرِينَ
9:37.en: Postponement (of a sacred month) is only an excess of disbelief whereby those who disbelieve are misled; they allow it one year and forbid it (another) year, that they may make up the number of the months which Allah hath hallowed, so that they allow that which Allah hath forbidden. The evil of their deeds is made fairseeming unto them. Allah guideth not the disbelieving folk

7:32.ar: قُلۡ مَنۡ حَرَّمَ زِينَةَ ٱللَّهِ ٱلَّتِيٓ أَخۡرَجَ لِعِبَادِهِۦ وَٱلطَّيِّبَٰتِ مِنَ ٱلرِّزۡقِۚ قُلۡ هِيَ لِلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ فِي ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا خَالِصَةࣰ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِۗ كَذَٰلِكَ نُفَصِّلُ ٱلۡأٓيَٰتِ لِقَوۡمࣲ يَعۡلَمُونَ
7:32.en: Say: Who hath forbidden the adornment of Allah which He hath brought forth for His bondmen, and the good things of His providing? Say: Such, on the Day of Resurrection, will be only for those who believed during the life of the world. Thus do we detail Our revelations for people who have knowledge

7:33.ar: قُلۡ إِنَّمَا حَرَّمَ رَبِّيَ ٱلۡفَوَٰحِشَ مَا ظَهَرَ مِنۡهَا وَمَا بَطَنَ وَٱلۡإِثۡمَ وَٱلۡبَغۡيَ بِغَيۡرِ ٱلۡحَقِّ وَأَن تُشۡرِكُواْ بِٱللَّهِ مَا لَمۡ يُنَزِّلۡ بِهِۦ سُلۡطَٰنࣰ ا وَأَن تَقُولُواْ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
7:33.en: Say: My Lord forbiddeth only indecencies, such of them as are apparent and such as are within, and sin and wrongful oppression, and that ye associate with Allah that for which no warrant hath been revealed, and that ye tell concerning Allah that which ye know not

VgrN0B1lcwk.speaker_note: 12th in his 'Achieving the Balance' series, speaks of his own fatwa caution and the 'haram police'
VgrN0B1lcwk.title: Achieving the Balance: Haram and Halal
VgrN0B1lcwk.one_line: Making haram halal is a grave wrong, but making halal haram is just as bad, and scholars say worse: it cheapens the real red lines.
VgrN0B1lcwk.summary: Opening with the verse against saying with your tongues 'this is halal and this is haram', the twelfth balance khutbah starts with the agreed part: Allah set boundaries, and turning the forbidden into the permitted ruins faith and community. A key role of Islamic education is to make those lines clear, as the Prophet said to do what he commands as far as you can but never cross what he forbids. He names two forces pushing the line today: normalization, where crossing once without visible consequence makes it routine, as with riba and the Arabs shifting the sacred months; and weakness, since the weak adopt the values of the strong. Haram means sacred, like the Sacred Mosque. Then the balance: making halal haram is equally wrong, and scholars considered it worse, citing the verse asking who forbade Allah's adornments. Overextending the list of prohibitions makes the next generation stop respecting all of them, as when a parent equates a haircut with drinking. He criticizes the 'haram police', checking every ingredient, and the history of banning TV, satellite dishes and the internet. Personal caution in grey areas is admirable but cannot be imposed on a community, since only Allah prohibits and the default is permissibility.

outline.heading: Opening
The twelfth balance
outline.gist: Liars against Allah do not succeed. Each talk in the series states something undisputed and then the piece needed to balance it, so that we become the nation of moderation Allah described.

outline.heading: Never make haram halal
outline.gist: Moderation needs exceptions and context; the definite part today is that turning the forbidden into the permitted can ruin faith, communities and the identity Allah gave us.

outline.heading: Has Allah given you permission?
outline.gist: Did Allah authorize you to declare things forbidden or allowed, or are you inventing as you go, and what do inventors expect on the Day of Judgment?

outline.heading: Make Allah's boundaries clear
outline.gist: A core function of Islamic institutions and education is making every Muslim clear on what is haram; the Prophet said to do what he commands as far as you can but never cross what he forbids.

outline.heading: Whoever crosses Allah's limits wrongs himself
outline.gist: Those who cross His boundaries and act as if they were not there wrong themselves and face painful punishment; no two Muslims dispute that Allah drew red lines.

outline.heading: Lawful by the word of Allah; a Muslim's sanctity
outline.gist: Spouses become lawful to each other only through Allah's word in a valid marriage, and every aspect of a fellow Muslim, his life, wealth and honour, is sacred.

outline.heading: Pushing the line
outline.gist: People nudge the line left and right: how haram can it be if everyone does it or the country has legalized it? He gives two reasons.

outline.heading: Reason one: normalization
outline.gist: Cross a red line once, nothing happens, so you cross it again until it feels normal and is hard to undo; those who consume riba end up saying trade is the same as riba.

outline.heading: Shifting the sacred months
outline.gist: The Arabs moved Muharram around to suit their wars; tampering with what Allah made sacred is an increase in disbelief.

outline.heading: Reason two: the weak adopt the values of the strong
outline.gist: Muslims today are weaker scientifically, academically and in numbers, so they feel they must take on others' values to seem civilized and progressive, just as others once took on Muslim values when Muslims were strong.

outline.heading: Haram means sacred
outline.gist: Killing and stealing are not up for debate; haram means sacred, as in al-Masjid al-Haram, a line you have no permission to cross.

outline.heading: The agreed part, in Arabic
outline.gist: He restates the first half in Arabic.

outline.heading: Making halal haram is just as bad
outline.gist: Forbidding the lawful is equally wrong and causes as many problems; scholars of merit consider it worse.

outline.heading: Who forbade Allah's adornment?
outline.gist: The Quran asks who dares forbid the adornment and good things Allah brought out for people, which are for believers and disbelievers in this life and for believers alone on the Day of Judgment.

outline.heading: Allah forbade specific things
outline.gist: Allah listed what He forbade, including speaking about Him without knowledge; calling things haram to be safe does not protect Islam.

outline.heading: A hundred red lines, respected by none
outline.gist: Turn a list of ten sacred lines into a hundred and people stop respecting all of them, becoming a leading reason people leave the faith.

outline.heading: A haircut is not alcohol
outline.gist: Telling a son a haircut you dislike is as haram as drinking or zina pushes him to do both; do not add culture, tradition or personal preference to what Allah forbade.

outline.heading: The haram police
outline.gist: Being extra careful in your own life is admirable, but you cannot force it on others or call things haram that are not; only Allah has that authority.

outline.heading: The default is permissibility
outline.gist: He thinks long before calling anything haram, since he would be prohibiting on Allah's behalf; the origin of everything is permissibility, and only specific things are forbidden.

outline.heading: The grey area
outline.gist: Between clear halal and clear haram are matters many do not know but scholars do; if you cannot ask, play it safe yourself, but do not stop someone who researched it.

outline.heading: Stop reading every ingredient
outline.gist: Skip the marshmallows with gelatin, but stop hunting through every label; it belittles the real prohibitions such as associating partners with Allah and indecency.

outline.heading: Zina is not an Oreo
outline.gist: Sexual relations outside marriage are an absolute line that cannot be equated with eating an Oreo; on lesser matters, go to people of knowledge and hear more than one opinion.

outline.heading: Raise children to know the real lines
outline.gist: Adding a million false prohibitions leaves him unable to protect the real ones; raise children to know exactly where the lines are and keep culture out of it.

outline.heading: Personal caution versus communal rulings
outline.gist: Avoiding something over a difference of opinion is godly, but communities cannot be held to it; he lived through internet, satellite dishes, TV and computers each being declared haram.

outline.heading: Every sheikh now has all four
outline.gist: Rushing to prohibit makes people disrespect the word haram; once a real line is crossed the way back is hard, so protect the lines by not adding to them.

outline.heading: Worse, but slower to show
outline.gist: Both errors are the same in their nature, and forbidding the lawful is worse; its consequences just take another generation to appear. He then restates the balance in Arabic.

outline.heading: The balance, in Arabic
outline.gist: He continues the restatement in Arabic.

outline.heading: Both errors are equally wrong
outline.gist: Permitting the forbidden and forbidding the permitted are equally wrong; his job is to keep reminding people of the real boundaries, which gets harder as more is added.

outline.heading: Second khutbah in Arabic
outline.gist: The second khutbah, given in Arabic.

N__Y9zatOA0.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Waqi'ah, Part 2: Verses 20-40
N__Y9zatOA0.one_line: Al-Waqi'ah 20-40: the rule on intoxicants, the forerunners' complete bliss, the people of the right, and why wealth demands more gratitude.
N__Y9zatOA0.summary: He notes that surahs have different structures and recaps how the Day of Judgment suddenly overturns the unspoken rules of worldly status, so people should bank on good deeds while relying on Allah's mercy. Prompted by the drink of Paradise that does not intoxicate, he sets out the fiqh: Islam forbids recreational intoxication in any amount, including alcohol and recreational marijuana; medical anaesthesia is different, and tobacco and opioids are forbidden for their harm rather than as intoxicants, with the definition left to medical and legal experts. Preserving the mind is one of the five aims of Shariah, since reason is what makes us accountable. The forerunners receive whatever fruit and meat they desire, exclusive spouses, and the feeling that they earned it, with no idle talk, no reminders of past sins and no worry, which he calls the strongest force there is. The people of the right enjoy thornless lote trees, bananas, extended shade, flowing water and fruit never forbidden, unlike Adam's tree. Their share is equal among early and later generations, while later forerunners are fewer because ease brings less gratitude, as the companions lamented. He urges Muslims to become wealthy and pour it into masjids and the needy, since the patient poor are rewarded without reckoning while those given more are expected to do more.

outline.heading: How surahs are structured
outline.gist: Some build to a central verse, some alternate stories and commentary; most, like Al-Waqi'ah, are paragraphs viewing one theme from different angles.

outline.heading: The unspoken rules of worldly status
outline.gist: Wealth, academics, politics, family name and who you know add up to status, and people who miss these cues struggle.

outline.heading: A sudden reshuffle that only the prepared survive
outline.gist: Some unknown in this world rise and some respected fall; its suddenness is what hurts, unless you already know what status will rest on.

outline.heading: What you bank on is gone
outline.gist: Wealth, connections and youth disappear; bank on good deeds while ultimately relying on Allah's mercy.

outline.heading: What makes you feel valuable each day?
outline.gist: A Muslim should feel a day was good by how close it brought him to Allah, not by money or career progress.

outline.heading: Recap: drink without headache or intoxication
outline.gist: The surahs from Qaf onward have little fiqh, but this verse warrants a ruling.

outline.heading: Recreational intoxication is haram
outline.gist: Khamr comes from covering the mind; anything that intoxicates for fun is forbidden, while medical anaesthesia is not.

outline.heading: Any amount of alcohol, and marijuana
outline.gist: Even under one percent still intoxicates; recreational cannabis is haram, prescribed medical cannabis is a separate last-resort matter.

outline.heading: Tobacco and opioids: haram for a different reason
outline.gist: Scholars leave the definition of intoxicant to medicine; nicotine is not one, but smoking kills, and opioids are forbidden recreationally for their harm.

outline.heading: Every substance carries a tax
outline.gist: Nothing you put into your body is benign, so take substances only on sound professional advice.

outline.heading: The five things Shariah preserves
outline.gist: Life, faith, dignity, wealth and the mind.

outline.heading: The mind makes you accountable
outline.gist: Removing your judgment on purpose does not remove responsibility; whatever you do drunk is fully your fault.

outline.heading: Find life's highs while sober
outline.gist: Intoxicated feelings are not real, need ever more and breed addiction; real living finds joy without them.

outline.heading: No, cannabis is not permitted after Isha
outline.gist: A rumour attributed a permissive fatwa to him; it is haram at any time, and a Muslim should eventually accept it because Allah said so.

outline.heading: Fruit and the meat of birds as they desire
outline.gist: In Paradise the forerunners choose whatever they want.

outline.heading: In this world we eat by halal, not desire
outline.gist: Check not only ingredients but that the money was earned and the food bought lawfully.

outline.heading: Spouses like hidden pearls
outline.gist: Full intimacy comes from exclusivity: no one has had access to your spouse or to you.

outline.heading: Keeping intimacy alive in marriage
outline.gist: After marriage people get lazy and stop making each other feel special, which kills affection; it takes effort.

outline.heading: A reward for what they used to do
outline.gist: We do not truly deserve it, but Allah tells us we do so the pleasure is psychologically complete, unlike a partner who keeps reminding you that you did not earn it.

outline.heading: No idle talk and no reminders of sin
outline.gist: Laghw is talk you do not care about; ta'thim is being reminded of past mistakes; only words of peace are heard.

outline.heading: Worry, the strongest thing, is removed
outline.gist: A classical chain of what overcomes what ends with deep worry stronger than sleep; one remembered problem can ruin a day, and Paradise removes it.

outline.heading: Reciting the second group's passage with tajweed notes
outline.gist: Common errors with the noon and meem, and stopping on tanween fath after a hamzah with an alif in Hafs.

outline.heading: The people of the right
outline.gist: The rhetorical question says no language can fully describe their joy.

outline.heading: Lote trees with the thorns removed
outline.gist: The sidr smells beautiful but has thorns; you already lived a life with thorns and persevered, so the harm is plucked out.

outline.heading: Bananas, and a scholar who loved them
outline.gist: Talh are banana trees, rare in Arabia and the Levant; a classical scholar known for dressing well out of respect for knowledge loved bananas, and so does he.

outline.heading: Seventeen fruits around his childhood home
outline.gist: Counting the fruit trees around his village showed him how blessed he was; pomegranates were so prized that his uncle chased him over a missing one.

outline.heading: Bananas were a luxury
outline.gist: Buying a kilo was news in the village, which is why the Quran names fruits its first listeners valued.

outline.heading: The Quran speaks in what its listeners knew
outline.gist: Camels and certain fruits are named because Arabs knew them; extrapolate to whatever you enjoy.

outline.heading: Extended shade
outline.gist: No running from a burning sun; you live where it is cool and easy.

outline.heading: Water poured out
outline.gist: Abundant water meant much to desert Arabs and may matter again if the Great Lakes dry up.

outline.heading: Fruit neither cut off nor forbidden
outline.gist: Adam left Paradise over one forbidden tree; in this world we practise self-control over what is forbidden for our own good, so nothing is forbidden there.

outline.heading: Raised couches and spouses created anew
outline.gist: High furnishings with a view; spouses perfectly formed, exclusive, loving and of the same age.

outline.heading: An equal share from early and later generations
outline.gist: Unlike the forerunners, the people of the right come equally from both; later forerunners are fewer because more ease brings less gratitude.

outline.heading: Tested with ease and not grateful enough
outline.gist: Companions who died owning almost nothing wept that they were patient in hardship but less grateful in ease.

outline.heading: Become wealthy and pour it where it is needed
outline.gist: Masjid boards arguing over a few thousand dollars is pathetic; make money to fund masjids, education, mental health and the underprivileged.

outline.heading: The patient pass without reckoning
outline.gist: Everyone will be questioned about time, youth, wealth and knowledge, but those who persevered through hardship walk past like VIPs.

outline.heading: Given more, expected to do more
outline.gist: No one wants poverty and disease, but those with much have much to lose and often turn mediocre.

outline.heading: Hoping for the first group, fearing the third
outline.gist: He admits he postpones the verses on the third group because they frighten him, and that fear should motivate.

eQ2SW5HdnlE.speaker_note: 13th or 14th in his 'Achieving the Balance' series; coins 'Aladdin's lamp syndrome' and tells personal stories
eQ2SW5HdnlE.title: Achieving the Balance: Dua (Supplication)
eQ2SW5HdnlE.one_line: Allah always responds to dua, but response is not delivery on demand; dua needs certainty, effort, constant conversation and total honesty.
eQ2SW5HdnlE.summary: This balance khutbah begins with the undisputed point: Muslims are commanded to call on Allah, and He always responds. Al-Fatiha is itself a dua, the verse in the fasting passage skips the usual 'say' to show Allah is near without an intermediary, and dua is the core of all worship, made with certainty; refusing to make it is arrogance. The balance comes in five points. First, Allah promised to respond, not to give exactly what you ask when you ask; He may give later, give something better, avert harm or store reward for the Hereafter. Treating dua like a genie is what he calls Aladdin's lamp syndrome, and he says none of his own duas were ever granted exactly as asked. Second, do not build faith on one answered dua, since it collapses at the first unanswered one. Third, dua without effort is borderline disrespectful, like a single man praying for children; the Prophet prayed desperately at Badr while also fighting. Fourth, dua is a lifelong conversation that tells Allah who you are and what you value, and those with Allah are never lonely. Fifth, take off the mask: speak to Allah as the weak, sinful person you really are, which is a therapeutic breakthrough.

outline.heading: Opening
The balance series
outline.gist: Each talk explains an undisputed Islamic concept, then the caveat or exceptions needed to practise it properly; the series has covered almost every area of Islamic life.

outline.heading: Al-Fatiha is a dua
outline.gist: No Muslim doubts that we are commanded to call on Allah at all times and that He responds; the first thing a Muslim learns, Al-Fatiha, is itself a dua.

outline.heading: I am near, with no 'say'
outline.gist: 'Call on Me and I will respond.' In the fasting passage Allah answers the question about Himself directly, skipping the usual 'say' to show there is no intermediary: I am near and answer the caller.

outline.heading: Who answers the distressed?
outline.gist: Who answers the one in desperate need and removes hardship when you are scared and weak, and is there any god besides Allah? Yet we forget so quickly.

outline.heading: He gives more than you asked
outline.gist: He answers those who believe and do good and adds from His bounty; call on Him humbly, openly or quietly, wherever you are.

outline.heading: Dua is the core of worship
outline.gist: Dua is worship: break any ritual down, prayer or recitation, and at its heart is speaking to Allah.

outline.heading: Ask with certainty; refusing is arrogance
outline.gist: Ask with certainty He will answer, since He does not answer a distracted heart; not making dua is a sin and an act of arrogance, and Allah always responds.

outline.heading: The agreed part, in Arabic
outline.gist: He calls this an agreed maxim and restates it in Arabic.

outline.heading: Point one: He said 'respond', not 'give'
outline.gist: Not getting what you asked does not mean He did not respond; the Quran says 'I will respond', never 'I will give you what you ask'.

outline.heading: The many forms of a response
outline.gist: Sometimes He gives what you want now, sometimes later, sometimes what you need instead, sometimes He averts a harm, and sometimes He keeps it for the Day of Judgment.

outline.heading: Aladdin's lamp syndrome
outline.gist: You are answered as long as you are not hasty and say you asked and got nothing; dua is not a genie's lamp, and expecting it to be ends in disappointment that is your own fault.

outline.heading: None of his duas came as asked
outline.gist: Not once has he received exactly what he asked when he asked; he got it later, differently and better, and saw that what he wanted would have ruined him.

outline.heading: Point two: do not build iman on one dua
outline.gist: Belief that rests on one answered prayer collapses the first time a prayer is not granted the way you wanted.

outline.heading: A building on a twig
outline.gist: Iman is built on the signs in the universe, history and your own life, all pointing to one Creator; he has seen people question God after one unanswered dua, though He never promised instant delivery.

outline.heading: Point three: dua without action is borderline disrespectful
outline.gist: Asking Allah for the ummah's success while doing nothing toward it is a problem.

outline.heading: 'You do it, I'm busy'
outline.gist: Dua with no effort, plan or intention, outside any movement to get it done, amounts to telling Allah to do it because you are too busy.

outline.heading: A single man praying for children
outline.gist: After he made a specific Ramadan dua for the ummah, a wise man told him it was like a single man asking Allah for children: get married first.

outline.heading: The Prophet's dua at Badr: working towards it
outline.gist: Show Allah you care: at Badr the Prophet begged for the promised victory until his cloak fell and Abu Bakr reassured him, while working day and night. We make dua and go home with no plan; the phrase to take away is 'working towards it'.

outline.heading: Point four: a constant conversation
outline.gist: Dua is staying in touch; people invented social media because they hate being alone, and loneliness can ruin a person.

outline.heading: Check on the lonely
outline.gist: Spend time with people who are lonely and struggling; it can pull someone out of a dark place. Those who have Allah are never lonely, and dua tells Him what you hope for.

outline.heading: Your dua shows what you value
outline.gist: Since you only ask for good, your dua reveals what your life is about: worldly wishes are allowed, but asking for Jannah and to stop sinning tells Him who you are.

outline.heading: Asking to be better
outline.gist: Asking to be a better child, parent, spouse and person shows you know what is right, which you can plead on the Day of Judgment; pick up the phone and never put it down, and start preparing for Ramadan.

outline.heading: What is worth asking for?
outline.gist: If you were to meet Allah, what would be worth asking? The early Muslims asked Him for everything, even a shoe strap, but thought about what was worth the conversation.

outline.heading: Dua is therapeutic
outline.gist: Dua is not about getting things but speaking to Allah and voicing your fears, which is deeply therapeutic, and that leads to a fifth point he had not planned.

outline.heading: Point five: begging, not an interview
outline.gist: Dua is not a formal interview; we make it in sujood, the most humbled position, begging the King of kings, as the Prophet raised his hands until his armpits showed.

outline.heading: Take off the mask
outline.gist: Do not recite memorized formulas; peel off the persona and speak as who you are, since He sees right through you. It is sad if the mask has fused to your face.

outline.heading: Speak as the weak, sinful servant you are
outline.gist: No one needs to teach you how to cry in dua; speak honestly as a scared, tired, sinful servant who should be better, and the tears come.

outline.heading: Not the way you speak to your boss
outline.gist: If people knew who he really was, they would not let him on the minbar, and that is true of everyone; no one knows us but Allah, so do not hide from Him.

outline.heading: Honesty is the breakthrough
outline.gist: Admitting you are helpless, lost and scared and turning to Allah is a breakthrough you could otherwise spend thousands on a psychiatrist to reach.

outline.heading: One ungranted wish among countless gifts
outline.gist: Abandoning Allah over one thing you did not get, while ignoring everything else He gave, is arrogance and entitlement you would not accept from your own child.

outline.heading: The five points in review
outline.gist: Allah always responds, though not always with what you asked; do not rest iman on one answered dua; work towards what you ask; never stop the conversation; and speak to Him without the persona.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Dua and invocation
themes.note: Dua is commanded and always answered, but answers take many forms; impatience and genie-like expectations are the problem.

themes.label: Tawakkul: reliance on Allah
themes.note: Dua must be paired with action and a plan; the phrase to take away is 'working towards it'.

themes.label: Mental health, anxiety and emotional wellbeing
themes.note: Loneliness can ruin people; spend time with those who are isolated. Honest dua is deeply therapeutic.

themes.label: Dua and invocation
themes.note: Dua as a constant conversation that reveals your values, made humbly in sujood rather than formally.

themes.label: Self-honesty and self-accountability (muhasabah)
themes.note: Drop the public persona with Allah, who sees through it; admitting weakness and sin is the real breakthrough.

themes.label: Gratitude (shukr) and appreciation
themes.note: Ignoring countless blessings over one ungranted request is entitlement you would not accept from your own child.

quran.point: The whole surah is a dua, the first thing a Muslim learns.
Call upon Me and I will respond to you.
When My servants ask about Me, I am near: Allah answers without the usual 'say'.
Who answers the distressed when they call and removes hardship? Yet you forget quickly.
He answers those who believe and do good and gives them more from His bounty.
Call on your Lord humbly and privately, openly or quietly.
Those too arrogant to call on Him face punishment: not making dua is a sin.

hadith.gist: Dua is worship.
Call on Allah certain of His answer; He does not answer a heedless, distracted heart.
Allah answers dua in different ways: granting it, averting a harm, or storing it for the Hereafter.
You are answered as long as you are not hasty and say 'I prayed and was not answered'.
At Badr the Prophet begged Allah for the promised victory until his cloak fell and Abu Bakr told him Allah would not abandon him.
Dua is answered as long as one does not ask for sin.
The early Muslims asked Allah for everything, even a shoe strap.
The servant is closest to his Lord in prostration; the Prophet raised his hands in dua until his armpits showed.

maxims: Aladdin's lamp syndrome
He said 'I will respond', not 'I will give'
Iman built on one dua is a building on a twig
Dua without amal is borderline disrespectful
Working towards it
Take off the mask when you speak to Allah

stories.who: His own duas
stories.point: Not one was granted exactly as and when he asked; in hindsight what he wanted would have ruined him.

stories.who: A wise man after his Ramadan dua
stories.point: Asking for the ummah's success without working for it is like a single man asking Allah for children.

stories.who: The Prophet's dua at Badr
stories.point: Desperate, heartfelt dua was paired with full effort in the field.

contemporary: Social media as a sign of the human need to stay connected; widespread loneliness
Honest dua compared with spending thousands of dollars on a psychiatrist
takeaways: Make dua constantly and with certainty that Allah responds
Do not judge Allah's response by whether you got what you asked when you asked
Pair every dua with real effort toward it
Reach out to people around you who are lonely
Speak to Allah honestly as who you are, and prepare what you will ask for in Ramadan
